sections.title: About the project
sections.body:
Cloudchipr is a cloud costs observability, management and automation platform.

It helps engineering and finance teams save time and money by automating cloud operations. With Cloudchipr, teams can schedule different automated workflows that send Slack alerts, build Tableau charts, create Jira tickets, and deactivate unused resources across all major cloud platforms. It’s like Zapier for cloud ops.

sections.title: How it started
sections.body:
Imagine being a UX designer exploring the world of cloud systems like AWS, GCP, and Azure. Sounds hard ha?

I joined a team of expert SRE and DevOps engineers when the project was just starting, moving from being a solo designer. Back then, all we had were a concept and a few rough mockups. As I was relatively new to this field, I decided to start with the basics – fundamental learning. This study covered a series of important steps that I needed to work through.

sections.title: Field Study

sections.body: I enrolled in a course on Udemy (218 lectures in total). Think of it as a crash course in cloud language and landscape. It helped me understand the jargon and navigate the territory better.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.body:
We have seen 1000s of 💸 per Hour of cloud waste paid for years just because:

Companies waste a large percentage of their cloud cost to pay for resources that are never used.
Developers forget to cleanup after tests.
Automation tools fail in the middle of execution and leave the cloud resources.
Finances and business do not have context whether the growing cloud cost is a waste.

Based on the personal research and information gathered from interviewing company’s founders and key stakeholders there is a clear need for a strong cost optimization platform that can effectively address the issue of wasting thousands of dollars per hour.

sections.title: Problem Discovered During User Research
sections.body: Every day, SRE and DevOps teams face a common issue - the considerable effort they put into cost optimization. This involves a lot of work to make sure things are efficient and cost-effective in the cloud. However, there's also the challenge of human errors that comes into play. Sometimes, mistakes happen, like setting things up wrong or not managing resources properly. These errors can undo the hard work of cost optimization, making the job more complicated for SRE and DevOps teams.

sections.title: Competitor Analysis
sections.body:
When looking at other companies in the field, I did two kinds of analysis: direct and indirect competitors. For direct competitors, I checked out companies with similar products or services as ours. I looked at what they offer, how much they charge, and who they target. This helped me see how we compare in terms of strengths and weaknesses.

Indirect competitors were a bit different. These are companies that might not do exactly what we do, but they could still take customers away. I researched them to understand their potential impact on our market.

I did a lot of research, reading reports, and checking what customers say online. This gave me a good sense of what people like and don't like about our competitors. And I didn't just stop at that. I also looked into the technology they use and any unique things they offer. In the end, all this info helped me figure out where we stand compared to others and how we can stand out.

sections.title: To Design or Not to Design system?
sections.body:
The company has tasked me with determining whether to purchase license of on of the existing design systems or to create a new one. Beyond the pros and cons that contribute to this decision, there's an effective approach I've undertaken – calculating the Return on Investment (ROI) for developing our own design system. This analytical method provides a clear and strategic means of comprehending the optimal direction to take.

Total ROI for One Project
ROI = Cost Savings - Cost of Design System Implementation
$8000 - $20,000 = -$12,000

The decision was clear-cut. After thorough research among various available solutions, we concluded that MUI was the ideal choice.

sections.title: About project
sections.body: Material Exchange is a digital platform that facilitates the efficient and streamlined exchange of material information between brands, manufacturers, and suppliers in the fashion and footwear industry.

sections.caption: Initial wireframes of single material page.

sections.title: Discovery Phase
sections.body:
Imagine Nike's material manager journeying to Vietnam, seeking sustainable materials to be used as a small peace for Air Jordans. Collaborating with local suppliers, they usually assess quality, recycling, and sustainability, incurring costs of $15,000 for travel and $10,000 for testing. This risk underscores Nike's commitment to responsible sourcing (only 15% of positive findings).

Companies like Nike spend millions on such research, but just a fraction proves valuable. So, material digitalization is needed for cost savings. The potential to revolutionize sourcing and sustainability drives ongoing innovation.

sections.caption: A tour of the Goodwill Outlet warehouse and retail store in St. Paul, MN, in April 2019.

sections.body:
Fashion is responsible for 10 percent of human-caused greenhouse gas emissions and 20 percent of global wastewater, and uses more energy than the aviation and shipping sectors combined. Global fashion also consumes 93 billion metric tons of clean water each year, about half of what Americans drink annually.

Since the 2000s, fashion production has doubled and it will likely triple by 2050, according to the American Chemical Society. Ninety-two million tonnes of unwanted fabrics are disposed of each year, and 14.5 million tons of textiles were landfilled and incinerated in 2018.

Leftover fabrics have already been produced, so there is no expenditure of water, energy, or virgin raw materials to create something new. With Material Exchange, they are available and accessible on a global level for brands to use in upcoming collections.

sections.caption: Screenshot of “Deadstock Depot”. Online services allows to sell purchase deadstock fabrics.

sections.title: User Research
sections.body: To ensure a user-centered approach to our decisions, I conducted a comprehensive survey to validate our assumptions about Material Exchange. With an impressive participation of 160 individuals from 24 different countries, we gained valuable insights into the needs and preferences of our user base. Analyzing the survey data allowed us to confirm our assumptions, identify common trends, and prioritize improvements based on user feedback.

We made it a practice to conduct iterative user interview and testing sessions at least twice a month. This involved engaging both new users and maintaining connections with existing ones. At first, we experimented with recruiting users through the usertesting.com platform. However, we soon realized that custom user recruitment is significantly more effective. Platform users often exhibit strong biases that can impact the quality of our insights.

Combining insights from various sources—company strategy, user research, quantitative surveys, and competitive analyses—we crafted our initial hypothetical personas. This marked the beginning of our ongoing process to discover new user archetypes throughout the journey.

sections.title: Building the Visual Language
sections.body: To create the complete Design language of the product, we initially concentrated on designing specific components unique to the product, such are material swatches and folders.

sections.title: Iconography
sections.body: Due to time constraints and the absence of a dedicated graphic designer on the team, we gathered icons from various collections and then harmonized them into a unified style. As a result we made a font of 350 pixel perfect linear icons including 43 industry specific.
After 2.5 months of dedicated effort, the Mat-EX design system was baked and handed over to the development team.

sections.title: Ideation Phase
sections.body: As a design lead, I often took part in ideation sessions. These sessions involved more than just coming up with user-centered solutions; I also facilitated prioritization discussions, design sprints and other related activities.

sections.caption: Screenshot of “User Value/Satisfaction Matrix” building session.

columns.body:
• How might we effectively centralize and organize digital materials and assets, providing easy searchability and accessibility for brands, manufacturers, and suppliers within the Material Exchange platform?
  • How might we enhance collaboration and communication between teams by integrating feedback and approval processes seamlessly within the Material Exchange platform, ensuring efficient collaboration and minimizing miscommunication?
  • How might we assist brands in maintaining consistent and cohesive material usage across different teams and stakeholders, leveraging the Material Exchange platform’s capabilities?

• How might we automate manual tasks and streamline workflows within the Material Exchange platform to significantly improve efficiency, saving valuable time for all users involved?
  • How might we ensure robust access controls and permissions within the Material Exchange platform, prioritizing data security and confidentiality to protect sensitive information?
  • How might we provide valuable analytics and insights on material usage and performance within the Material Exchange platform, empowering data-driven decision-making for brands, manufacturers, and suppliers?
  • How might we guarantee seamless scalability and integration of the Material Exchange platform with other tools and systems used by brands, manufacturers, and suppliers, ensuring smooth operations and compatibility?

columns.title: Personalized Dashboard
columns.body: Centralized interface that offers users an instant overview of their material assets. It provides real-time insights into the status, location, and usage of materials, streamlining inventory management and enhancing decision-making.

columns.title: Smart Search
columns.body: Smart Search empowers users to quickly and intelligently locate specific materials within their inventory. Using advanced search algorithms and filters, it understands user queries and offers real-time suggestions as users type, making the search process highly efficient.

sections.title: Material managers struggle, spending too much time adding materials to folders.
sections.body:
🕒 Exp. Duration — 45 min
❌ Act. Result — 61 min

In a usability test, a material manager was asked to create a winter-fall collection of materials. This involved making folders for different categories and then finding and adding materials to those folders.

Interestingly, a lot of time was spent opening and closing folders repeatedly. The manager also had to add each material individually, which took up a large portion of the session.

Surprisingly, about 60% of the total time was used just for managing folders and adding materials. This left only 40% for more important work such as decision-making and evaluating materials.

As a solution, we introduced an innovative feature named “Dropzone”. Drawing inspiration from people's familiarity with operating system folders, Dropzone enables users to effortlessly drag and drop files, mirroring a natural experience.

To enhance efficiency, we added the capability to select multiple items and utilize multiple dropzones, streamlining the process of managing up to 4 folders within a single task. This approach not only simplifies the user experience but also significantly accelerates the material management process.

🕒 Exp. Duration — 45 min
🎉 Act. Result — 23 min
Users frequently conduct similar searches, resulting in repetitive manual entry of search criteria and potential frustration due to redundancy.

Easier grouping of search criteria would simplify repetitive operations by enabling users to execute the same search with a single click. To address this need, we introduced and tested the “Save Search” feature.

sections.title: Why Are Some Materials Overlooked by Brands? The Influence of Image Editing Knowledge and Budget Constraints
sections.body:
During my regular observations and interviews with users from various backgrounds, I noticed a consistent pattern: Brands paid more attention to materials that looked good with attractive images and well-designed cards. This phenomenon is known as the Aesthetic Usability Effect, where people tend to judge content based on its appearance.

And here's the catch: Because of this phenomenon, brands didn't seem to pay as much attention to materials that didn't meet their visual standards. To understand why, I dug deeper.

After engaging in discussions with users, I understood the root cause of this unexpected behavior. It became obvious that many suppliers, especially smaller ones and individuals, faced significant challenges due to their limited image editing skills and budget constraints. These constraints prevented them from effectively utilizing quality image editing tools.

It's important to note that image editing softwares like Photoshop are quite complex for basic operations, such are crop or resize an image, and many material managers either aren't familiar with it or lack access due to licensing limitations.

sections.title: Objective
sections.body: Our objective is to enhance the Material Exchange Marketplace's image presentation capabilities by providing easy and intuitive design tool for material managers.

sections.title: Anticipated Transformations: The Impact of Our Image Editing Tool on Material Exchange
sections.body:
• With the implementation of our tool, we anticipate a substantial increase in material engagement. We predict that materials edited using our platform will experience a 30% boost in engagement, piquing the interest of brands and users alike.
  • Our analysis suggests that materials with professionally edited images and well-designed cards will exhibit a 20% improvement in conversion rates compared to non-enhanced materials.
  • With the tool now available, we anticipate attracting and onboarding a larger number of small suppliers and individuals. Our projections indicate a 40% growth in our supplier base within the first year of tool implementation.
  • We predict a significant enhancement in user satisfaction as a direct result of this tool. We anticipate that 90% of our users will report an improved experience, noting that the tool makes it easier for them to create visually appealing materials.
  • Brands are expected to demonstrate heightened interest in materials from a more diverse set of suppliers, including smaller businesses and individuals. Our projections indicate a 25% increase in brand interactions with these suppliers.

sections.title: the Project
sections.body: Hotel Apartments is a flexible online booking service specializing in extended-stay hotel room bookings. Easily browse and book carefully selected serviced apartments and villas, providing you with spacious, budget-friendly, and all-inclusive lodging options.

metadata.label: Services:
metadata.value: Field Studies, User Research, Competitive analyses, UI Design, Usability testing

sections.title: According to official statistics, the number of Russian citizens living in Dubai increased by 170% between February and June 2022.
sections.body:
Since the start of the Russian-Ukrainian War in February 2022, there has been a significant increase in the number of Russians moving to Dubai.

A number of companies have opened offices in Dubai and financed their employees’ relocation along with their families including:

  • Visa
  • Alphabet Inc's Google
  • Talnet, a company matching tech workers from Eastern Europe with startups worldwide

Hotel apartments offer them a flexible, convenient, and comfortable living arrangement as they navigate the challenges of relocation. With fully furnished spaces, on-site amenities, and services tailored to their needs, hotel apartments not only ease the transition but also foster a sense of community and support in a new and unfamiliar environment.

sections.title: Field Studies
sections.body:
Since the hotel industry was new to me, I began with a field study. I embarked on a business trip where my client had invited me to their had office in Dubai. The objective was to immerse myself in the world of hotel apartment rental services, understand the competitive landscape, and conduct user research to document the primary pain points and challenges faced by potential and existing customers.

Upon arriving at the airport in Dubai, I was greeted by Shabahir Ibn Muhammad, the Guest Relations Officer (GRO): one of the key stakeholders in this business. During our one-hour trip to my apartment, I started interviewing him because I knew he had important insights. We talked about the challenges guests faced, their preferences, and how the company helped them. This was my first step in understanding the hotel apartment rental industry in Dubai.

sections.title: Walking a Mile in the User's Shoes
sections.body: As the website already existed, one of my main goals was to understand the current customer experience and identify the issues that led to drop-offs (87%), as well as why some users chose competitors over our service. In meetings and interviews with users who visited our office in person, I asked them to replicate their actions on our website, offering them gifts that I had brought with me from Yerevan (magnets, candies, etc.).

sections.title: Findings
sections.body:
• Many users found it frustrating that they couldn't book a hotel apartment instantly. Instead, they had to send an inquiry and wait for a response.
  • Users had trouble finding similar properties when they used specific filters that resulted in no search results.
  • People planning long stays cared a lot about knowing facilities around the place they're booking, especially if they have children and need to find schools. They were also concerned about extra costs, like transportation.
  • Users wanted to know exactly how much they'd be paying, including all bills, right from the start.

sections.title: The Brand
sections.body: Even when you're reselling hotel apartments, it's important to have your own special style and appearance. This helps you create a distinct identity and attract customers.

sections.title: Tempo
sections.subtitle: One courier route for food, pharmacy items, documents, and custom requests.

sections.title: the Project
sections.body:
Tempo brings food, pharmacy items, documents, and custom errands into one delivery app. Its signature feature lets a customer combine several pickup points in one courier route, review the order of stops, and track the full delivery from one place.

I worked with the product team on the experience strategy, information architecture, core flows, interface design, and a reusable UI kit.

sections.title: Several errands often happen at the same time
sections.body:
A customer may order dinner while an important document waits across town. Standard delivery apps treat each request as a separate order, with another checkout, courier, fee, and tracking screen.

Tempo needed one flow that could combine different request types without making the route feel complex. Customers had to understand where the courier would go, how another stop affected the trip, and when the full order would arrive.

sections.title: One order, several stops, one courier
sections.body:
Customers add food, documents, pharmacy items, or a custom address to the same delivery. Tempo groups those stops, proposes an efficient order, and keeps the route visible before checkout.

The product explains the benefit in context. A time-saving message appears on the map, while the route sheet lists each stop and lets the customer adjust the plan before the courier starts.

items.label: Study delivery apps and route planners
Map categories, orders, and multi-stop journeys
Test the route model in wireframes
Build the product UI and component library
Let customers manage different delivery needs in one app
Show each stop, route change, and arrival expectation
Make another pickup feel like part of the current order
Give the team reusable patterns for new categories

sections.title: Delivery apps taught us conventions. Route planners taught us sequence.
sections.body:
We reviewed local delivery products to understand familiar patterns for browsing, checkout, and tracking. We also studied route-planning tools because Tempo’s core interaction depends on ordering several locations.

The comparison exposed a gap. Delivery apps handled products well but treated each order as a closed journey. Route planners handled stops well but lacked the shopping context customers expect. Tempo needed both mental models in one interface.

sections.title: The plus button turns one delivery into a route
sections.body:
A customer can add another pickup without leaving the active order. The new address joins the route sheet, and Tempo updates the map and estimated time.

Contextual guidance introduces the feature at the moment it becomes useful. Customers learn the route model through the task rather than a separate tutorial.

columns.title: The route explains each decision
columns.body:
The map shows the pickup order and highlights the proposed path. A compact message estimates the time saved through optimization.

The bottom sheet keeps delivery details close to the map. Customers can inspect stops, change their order, and start the delivery without losing spatial context.

sections.title: Wireframes made the new route model testable
sections.body:
We mapped the path from category discovery to order building, route review, checkout, and tracking. Low-fidelity screens helped us decide where customers could add a stop and how the route sheet should respond.

The wireframes also connected supporting journeys such as sign-in, profiles, order history, and delivery preferences.

sections.title: Categories organize a broad service without hiding the route
sections.body:
Tempo covers food, pharmacy items, alcohol, shops, documents, and custom deliveries. Categories and filters help customers enter through the need they recognize.

The route remains the shared layer across those categories. A customer can move between shopping and delivery planning while the current stops stay intact.

sections.title: A consistent experience across different requests
sections.body:
Restaurant cards, pharmacy listings, document delivery, and custom pickups use the same product language. Customers keep familiar controls as the content changes.

Small choices support the wider service. Delivery preferences can reduce waste, saved information speeds up repeat orders, and account history keeps past routes accessible.

sections.title: Sensitive deliveries need more than a tracking dot
sections.body:
Document delivery introduced a stronger trust requirement. Customers need confirmation that the courier received the correct item and delivered it to the intended recipient.

Tempo pairs delivery status with clear addresses, recipient details, and confirmation messages. Sign-in and recovery flows offer familiar paths through email or phone, so customers can return to an active order without confusion.

columns.title: Launching the service before the app
columns.body:
The business needed a public entry point while the mobile product remained in progress. We designed a landing page that explains Tempo’s promise, gives customers a phone number for delivery requests, and invites couriers and partners to join.

The page let the team begin learning from real demand before the full application was ready.

sections.title: A system the product team can extend

items.label: Readable type for maps, commerce, and account flows
A green accent that connects brand and product
Spacing rules that hold across dense mobile screens
Reusable inputs, buttons, cards, feedback, and states

sections.title: The route is the product, not a final tracking screen
sections.body:
Tempo’s broad service catalog could have produced a collection of unrelated ordering flows. Treating the route as a persistent product layer gave those flows a shared structure.

The next design phase should test how customers interpret route changes, fees, and arrival estimates when they add more stops. Those decisions affect trust more than visual polish.

sections.title: iCredo
sections.subtitle: A conversational lending app designed to make a difficult financial decision feel understandable.

sections.title: The project
sections.body:
iCredo is a mobile AI chat experience for people exploring and managing a loan. It brings loan discovery, calculation, identity verification, repayment, and account status into one guided product.

The core design challenge was not simply to make an application easier to complete. It was to help a person understand a sensitive financial decision while the product collected the information required to make it.

metadata.label: Services:
metadata.value: Product strategy, UX, UI, design system

sections.title: The financial context made clarity essential

items.label: of surveyed people had never tried to take out a loan online
resident individual borrowers with active loan balances in Armenia
residents roughly carried an active loan balance
annual rate ceiling within the product context

sections.title: A necessary amount of information can still feel like too much
sections.body:
Many people were unfamiliar with online lending, while the product still had to collect detailed personal and financial information. In a high-interest, last-resort lending context, every request for information needed to feel deliberate, explainable, and respectful.

The existing web calculator treated borrowing as a calculation task. The mobile experience had to turn it into a guided decision journey.

columns.title: A conversation when context matters. Controls when precision matters.
columns.body:
The assistant asks for one decision at a time, explains why it is needed, and uses simple chat language. When a user needs accuracy—such as an amount or repayment preference—the conversation hands off to visible chips and structured inputs.

This avoids a long, impersonal form while keeping financial choices precise.

columns.title: Trust is designed into the verification flow
columns.body:
KYC gives users direct capture guidance, a clear task boundary, and a visible security-progress indicator. The experience makes it clear what is being requested, what has been completed, and what happens next.

The goal was not to make verification feel invisible. It was to make it feel understandable.

sections.title: What the first usability sessions were designed to challenge
sections.body:
Can a chat interaction make required questions feel clearer than a form? We tested whether people understood why the assistant was asking each question, especially when the request moved from a casual amount conversation into personal details.

Can people enter a number with confidence? The design pairs open input with quick amount choices and repayment modes, so users do not have to invent the interaction model themselves.

Can a person understand an active loan at a glance? The post-approval workspace brings loan status, remaining balance, progress, next payment, and repayment actions into one consistent view.

These are the validation hypotheses and design responses for the case-study draft. Replace this copy with documented session findings before presenting it as completed research.

columns.title: The loan remains legible after approval
columns.body:
My Loans turns a financial commitment into a manageable workspace. Cards show status, remaining balance, progress, next payment, repayment controls, and a route into detailed schedules.

The same component system carries the experience from first question through long-term management.

sections.title: A system for a product that keeps growing

items.label: Conversation patterns for guidance and decision making
Secure capture and clear step progress
Reusable account, repayment, status, and schedule patterns
Shared tokens, components, and mobile interaction rules

sections.title: Business context
sections.quote: Credo Finance’s stated goal is to give consumers a personal approach and flexible, convenient services. The product direction translated that goal into a mobile flow people could understand before they committed.

person.name: Bella Gabrielyan
person.role: Executive Director & Board Member, Credo Finance

sections.annotationText: Leadership context — not a direct testimonial

sections.title: The right interface does not make the decision disappear
sections.body:
Borrowing is personal, consequential, and sometimes stressful. The design did not try to hide that. It gave people a calmer way to ask questions, provide sensitive information, and keep track of what they had agreed to.

The strongest next step is to replace the validation hypotheses with documented usability-session notes and a before-and-after of the previous iCredo calculator.
